what_its_for: Venetoclax is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of blood cancers, including chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). It works by blocking a protein called BCL-2 that helps cancer cells survive, allowing the cancer cells to die.
how_to_take: Take venetoclax by mouth once a day with a meal and a full glass of water. Swallow the tablet whole — do not crush, break, or chew it. Try to take it at the same time every day. If you vomit after taking your dose, do not take another dose that day — just take your next dose at your regular scheduled time.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it over 5 weeks. This slow ramp-up schedule is very important to reduce the risk of a serious side effect called tumor lysis syndrome (TLS). A typical starting dose is 20 mg per day, increasing weekly to 50 mg, 100 mg, 200 mg, and finally 400 mg per day. Your exact dose may be different depending on your condition and other medicines you take. Never change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and it has been less than 8 hours since your scheduled time, take it as soon as you remember. If it has been more than 8 hours, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at your regular time the following day. Never take two doses in one day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store venetoclax tablets at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep them in the original container, away from heat, light, and moisture. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of the reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about proper medicine disposal.
what_to_avoid: Avoid eating grapefruit, grapefruit juice, Seville oranges, and starfruit while taking venetoclax, as they can increase the amount of this medicine in your body and raise the risk of side effects. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, including over-the-counter products, because many drugs can interact with venetoclax. Avoid getting live vaccines while on this medicine. Avoid large crowds or people who are sick, as venetoclax lowers your ability to fight infections.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: fever, chills, or signs of infection; rapid or irregular heartbeat; muscle cramps or spasms; nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that is severe; little or no urination; confusion or dizziness; unusual bleeding or bruising; shortness of breath; or swelling in your legs or feet. These could be signs of serious side effects like tumor lysis syndrome (TLS), low blood counts, or infection. Seek immediate help if you have trouble breathing or chest pain.
when_it_works: Venetoclax starts working right away in your body, but it may take several weeks to months before you or your doctor can see the full effects through blood tests or other measures. Your doctor will check your blood regularly to monitor how well the medicine is working and to watch for side effects. Do not stop taking venetoclax unless your doctor tells you to, even if you feel well.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Venetoclax can harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 30 days after the last dose. Men with female partners who can become pregnant should use birth control during treatment and for 30 days after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects and should be monitored closely by their doctor. Liver problems: If you have liver disease, your dose may need to be adjusted. Tell your doctor about any liver conditions you have. Kidney problems: Patients with reduced kidney function may have a higher risk of tumor lysis syndrome and will need extra monitoring, especially at the start of treatment.
